Use a sliding window and a map of each character’s latest position. For each right endpoint, if that character already occurs inside the window, move the left endpoint just past its previous occurrence—never backward—then update the map and maximum window length.

The invariant is that the current window contains no repeated characters and is the longest valid substring ending at the current position. Taking the maximum across those windows gives the overall answer, in O(n) time and O(k) space for k distinct characters.

Boundary cases: an empty string returns 0, one character returns 1, all identical characters return 1, and all distinct characters return the full length. The displayed examples give 3 for "abcabcbb" and 1 for "bbbbb"; "abba" gives 2 and checks that an old occurrence outside the window never moves the left endpoint backward. The screen does not specify Unicode character semantics, so code-unit versus code-point counting remains unspecified.

Sort intervals by ascending start, then scan from left to right. If the next start is at or before the current merged end, extend that end to the maximum of both ends; otherwise, finalize the current interval and begin a new one.

Invariant: after each step, the processed intervals are represented exactly by sorted, nonoverlapping merged intervals. Only the last merged interval can overlap the next interval, because starts are sorted.

Boundary cases: an empty input returns []; a single interval stays unchanged; nested or identical intervals collapse into one; touching intervals such as [1,2] and [2,3] merge into [1,3]. Unsorted input is handled by sorting, and a zero-length closed interval such as [2,2] follows the same overlap rule.

Time: O(n log n). Result space: O(n); sorting workspace depends on the implementation.

Approach: scan the rectangular grid. Each unvisited land cell starts a new island; increment the count and use iterative depth-first search to visit its entire component, checking only up, down, left, and right. Mark cells visited when pushing them onto the stack, using separate storage to preserve the input.

Invariant: after each completed traversal, every cell in that island is visited, and the count equals the number of components discovered. Each land cell is pushed at most once, so no island is counted twice.

Use bottom-up dynamic programming: set dp[0] = 0 and all other entries to infinity. For each total t from 1 through amount, consider every coin c ≤ t and minimize dp[t] using dp[t − c] + 1. Return dp[amount], or -1 if it remains infinite.

Invariant: after processing total t, every entry through t contains the fewest coins needed for that total, or infinity if unreachable. Every solution ends with some coin c; since denominations are positive, its remaining total t − c is smaller and already solved optimally. Coins can be reused without limit.

Boundary cases: amount 0 returns 0; no coins with a positive amount returns -1; coins larger than the current total are skipped. Unreachable totals such as coins [2], amount 3 return -1; duplicate denominations do not affect correctness. The attachment does not specify handling for negative or non-integer amounts.

Time: O(amount × coins.length). Space: O(amount).
